chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
title: The Vanguard band, its writing and Buddy Collette's advice
summary: Johnson praises the ten-piece band and its economical writing; Collette told Mingus to leave room for solos.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Yeah. I remember that -- seeing that band maybe five or six times, at least that many times, down at the Vanguard. I was absolutely knocked out with it. And Jerome Richardson and -- I remember, Richard Williams and Rolf Ericson and Charlie Mariano and -- who's the tenor player? Hafer
Dick Haneford.

Dick Hafer, yeah. He didn't play M. BASS CLARINET. any solos, he just had to play parts, mostly. And, boy, that was -- that just blew me away. And the trombone player was Butter, wasn't it? [Quentin JACKSON ed. note]
Yeah.

Man, that -- I thought to myself at the time that that probably is/close to a fully realized jazz performance by an ensemble as I'm ever going to hear. And I still haven't changed my mind about that. I mean, anybody can get clean-type performances, but that was so full of marvelous energy and people were just so responsive, and the record is so great, oh, just an incredible record.
I was very pleased, when I took -- wrote brought those tunes out for copyright, how economical all that writing was.
Economical?
Yeah. I mean, you used your materials to the fullest. It's not full of a lot of material. You were
very concise about the materials that you composed. And I think that's one of the reasons that that music is so great.
You're talking about the one with the ten-piece band.
Yeah.

Yeah, well, I learned something, because Buddy Collette came down and helped me with Town Hall. And he said, 'You've written too much music, man, you got to just open this up. Put some solos in. The guys don't have no chance to breathe, they're blowing -- reading all the time.' Said, 'You got all these guys on the stage with no solos.'
So I remembered that when I wrote the Town Hall -- I mean, for Village Vanguard.
Yeah.
I just opened it up.

Yeah, did you -- I mean, did you actively encourage people to get inside the music and -- because I remember, the players were really -- it was like Duke's band, the closest thing -- it was almost, like, better than Duke's band, because --
Those was just veterans. All the guys was just good musicians, that's all.
Yeah. But those guys are just bending and shaping the music. I mean, if you hear somebody really being himself in the baritone part, you know?
That was Jerome Richardson. (inaudible)?
Yeah.
Well, that was the reason for it. Jerome Drummer had a big sound, too.
